definition: Crack spreads can be traded either by assembling positions in the individual crude oil, gasoline, and diesel futures legs, or as a single packaged instrument (crack spread futures or options) listed directly on an exchange.
core_idea: Because a crack spread position is inherently less risky than any single outright leg, exchanges allow it to be margined and traded as one combined instrument, which is more capital-efficient than legging in with separate futures trades.
key_points: Every exchange futures trade requires margin sized to the risk of that trade
Building a crack spread from separate crude, gasoline, and diesel futures legs can tie up substantial capital across multiple margin positions
The combined crack spread is much less risky than holding any single underlying commodity outright, so less capital is required when it is margined as one unit
Exchanges commonly offer crack spread trading directly alongside markets for the underlying commodities
Crack spread futures and crack spread options are available on exchanges, replicating the same economic exposure as legging in manually
Exchange-listed crack instruments have lower margin requirements and execute all underlying legs simultaneously
relationships: Alternative execution method for the crack spread trades described above
trading_implications: Trading the exchange-listed crack instrument reduces margin/capital requirements and execution risk compared to manually legging into crude, gasoline, and diesel futures separately
